checked.label: who-years 6 years
problems: Holds. The abstract and results say 'Half of the cases of nicotine, alcohol, cannabis and cocaine dependence remitted approximately 26, 14, 6 and 5 years after dependence onset'. The headline now counts from first getting hooked, has 21 words and 1 figure, and says 'projected'. The methods say 'These projections were obtained by the standard actuarial method'.

The ellipsis quote keeps the source's words in order and drops the other drugs (rule 13). n=530 (Table 1, 'Cannabis Dependence (N=530)'). Remission means they 'finally stopped having any of these experiences (dependence criteria)'. NESARC 2001–2002, face-to-face. Males had lower remission hazards: adjusted HR 0.64 for weed. The limitations say institutionalized people 'may have not been sampled, leading to overestimation of the cumulative probability of remission'.

Note, no change: 'Weed was weaker in 2001 than today' does not come from this source. It is cautious, not hopeful. 'Free of it' could be read as 'off weed', but basis.measured says what free means, and the passed numbers 0 and 1 use the same wording.

checked.label: how-alone 54%
problems: Holds. Table 3 row: 'Cannabis (e.g., marijuana, hashish) | 45.8 | 5.53'. 100 − 45.8 = 54.2. The SE of 5.53 gives about ±11 points, so the 43–65% range in the caveat is right. Table 1 lists cannabis as primary substance at a weighted 11.0%, and 11% of 2,002 is about 220. Lifetime alcohol/substance use disorder diagnosis was 17.0%, about 1 in 6.

The 'assisted' definition (treatment, anti-relapse/craving medication, mutual-help, other community recovery support such as sober living) matches basis.measured. Table 2 lists 'Marijuana Anonymous (MA)'. Data were collected in July and August 2016 through the online KnowledgePanel. The limitations say the problem 'was participant-defined and did not necessarily signify the presence of a diagnosable AOD disorder', which matches the weak line. Headline: 16 words, 1 figure. Mirror: 10 words, second person.

checked.label: how-tries 2 tries
problems: Holds. Kelly 2019 Table 1: 'Cannabis | 4.62 (8.41) | 2 (1, 4) | 0, 100'. The new basis.measured wording ('including people who reported no serious try at all') matches the results: 'approximately 13% of the sample (n = 260) reported not making any serious recovery attempts'. The discussion says they 'did not count the current attempt'.

n: Kelly 2018 Table 1 headers read 'Cannabis (12.6%, n = 217)', with the footnote 'Displaying weighted counts', so 'a weighted count' is right. It is the same survey, July–August 2016. Headline: 13 words, 1 figure. Mirror: 12 words, second person.

checked.label: how-slips 71%
problems: Holds. The abstract has n=82 who 'achieved at least 2 weeks of abstinence during outpatient treatment for marijuana dependence', 71% lapsed within 6 months at an average of 73 days, and '71% of those who lapsed, relapsed to heavier use defined as at least 4 days of marijuana use in any 7-day period. Early lapses were more strongly associated with consequent relapse.' The new caveat matches this, and is no longer more hopeful than the source.
Headline: 17 words, 2 figures (71%, 6 months). The quote is word for word (23 words). 'Vermont' rests on the affiliation (University of Vermont, Burlington); the abstract names no site.

checked.label: helps-stop-vs-cut 63%
problems: Holds. The results say, word for word: 'However, 63% of CAN reported being abstinent from their primary substance (i.e., cannabis)'. Table 1b: 'From problem substance, % | 63.12'. The discussion says 'about one third of CAN reported continuing to use at least some cannabis despite resolving their cannabis problem', which supports 'the other 37% still used some'. The paper gives no time window for this row, so 'when asked' is right; its all-substances figure is 'in the past 90 days'.

Note, no change: Table 1b also has a row 'Current Cannabis Use, % | 29.54' for this group. That likely uses a shorter window than the abstinence row. The card does not cite it, and the authors' own 'about one third' matches 37%. Headline: 20 words, 2 figures. Mirror: 12 words. Minor: the caveat says twice that the problem was self-judged.

checked.label: helps-medicine 0 pills
problems: The headline holds: 'There are currently no pharmacotherapies approved for the treatment of cannabis use disorder'. THC preparations RR 1.04 (4 studies, 290) and N-acetylcysteine RR 1.17 (2 studies, 270) on abstinence at end of treatment against placebo. Headline: 22 words, 0 figures. n, the countries (USA 29, Australia 4, Israel 2, Canada 1, UK 1), the May 2024 search and the eligibility all match.

The caveat says 'the review calls the evidence uncertain'. For THC preparations and NAC the review rates the no-better result as 'moderate-certainty evidence'; 'the evidence is uncertain' goes with the cannabidiol and anticonvulsant results. The authors' conclusion is that the medicines 'should still be considered experimental'.
The caveat's last sentence, 'there is no '1 in N' figure yet', is jargon a reader cannot parse (rule 8), and names the format rule 12a keeps out of what-helps numbers. Dropped.

fix.caveat: Not proof that no medicine can help: most were tested in only a few small trials, and the review says all are still experimental. For THC medicines and NAC, it rates the no-better result as moderately certain.

checked.label: helps-talk 25 in 100
problems: The headline and big hold: 'abstinence rates were relatively low overall, with approximately one-quarter of participants abstinent at final follow-up'. Headline: 19 words, 1 figure. The quote is word for word (15 words). basis.n correctly says the review gives no count behind the one-quarter share; its point-prevalence comparison was 'six studies, 1166 participants'. The weak line fits the source's 'low and unstable'.

The caveat says therapy made people 'about 2.5 times as likely'. That is the ratio format rule 12a bans in the what-helps group ('never ×2.3'), and readers misread it. The build checks only big and headline, so it misses this. The abstract gives RR 2.55 and no per-100 figures. Replaced with a plain comparison that keeps 'weak' (the abstract calls it 'low-quality evidence').

Open doubt, no field change: rule 12a also wants a per-100 figure for people without therapy. The abstract has none. The full Cochrane review (PMC4914383) analysis tables may have event counts. Plan proof 4 (not in this recheck) uses the same '2.5 times' wording.

fix.caveat: At around 4 months, more people who had therapy said they weren't using than people who had little or none, but that evidence is weak. No kind of therapy clearly worked at 9 months or later. The 25 in 100 is a rough share across trials, not the gain over doing nothing.

checked.label: after-first-month Week 1
problems: The figure, n (62 vs 26, 55 of 62 with 30-day confirmed abstinence), ages 16–25, Boston, July 2015 – December 2016, weekly CANTAB tests and 54.4 of 90 days (Table 1) all hold. The quote matches the abstract word for word with an ellipsis. Headline: 20 words, 0 digit figures.

'Nobody was diagnosed' (caveat) and 'not diagnosed as hooked' (counted, weak) go beyond the source. The methods say 'Current and lifetime Axis I diagnoses were assessed with the Structured Clinical Interview for DSM-IV (SCID-IV) for participants recruited at the hospital'. The paper reports no weed-use diagnosis. That means it does not say, not that nobody had one. CUDIT mean 14.4 in the abstinence group.
'Attention did not' reads as attention not improving. In fact 'attention improved similarly in MJ-Abst and MJ-Mon', which the authors call 'consistent with a practice effect'.
The weak line says '62 who stopped'. 62 were assigned to stop; 55 stayed off all 30 days.
Open doubt for the build, no field change: the heavy-tag card label 'heavy users, not checked for addiction' is wrong here, because the CUDIT-R was given at the start.

fix.counted: regular weed users aged 16 to 25; no diagnosis of being hooked reported
fix.caveat: Memory improved more than in those who kept using; attention improved the same in both groups. Young users only. A weed-problem questionnaire was taken at the start, but the study reports no diagnosis and does not say how many were hooked. It could not say whether school or work results improved.
fix.weak: A small trial (62 asked to stop) of young users; the study reports no diagnosis of being hooked.

checked.label: after-mood 12 weeks
problems: The fixed basis fields hold. 'The trial was implemented at six sites across the U.S. between January 2014 and April 2015'. Participants were '302 adults (ages 18–50) with a diagnosis of cannabis dependence (per ... DSM-IV criteria) ... randomized to receive either N-acetylcysteine (NAC) 1200 mg or placebo twice daily, added to a contingency management (CM) and medication management platform'. CM vouchers 'targeted visit attendance and cannabis abstinence'. n=152 vs 150.

Headline: 21 words, 1 figure. It is a fair plain rendering of the authors' 'reduction in cannabis use is associated with reduction in anxiety and depression and improvement in sleep, on average'. Strictly, the result compares slopes between the two groups (Table 3), and the caveat says 'a link, not proof'. The quote is word for word (18 words).
Note, no change: 'the changes were small' (caveat, weak) is the drafter's reading of the slope coefficients (about −0.1 per week). The paper does not say it, but it is cautious, not hopeful.

checked.label: stuck: I've smoked for years. I'm stuck.
problems: Holds. The proof is 40 words, says 'projected', and puts the counted 344 of 530 first (rule 10). Table 1: 'Cannabis Dependence (N=530)'. Tables 3 and 4: 'Cannabis remission (N=344)'. Both quotes are word for word: 'Half of cannabis dependence remissions occurred approximately 6 years after dependence onset among Whites and Blacks, 5 years among Hispanics and NH/PI and 7 years among AI/AN' (results) is 27 words, or 29 by the build count.
The 'Free' line matches the remission question ('finally stopped having any of these experiences (dependence criteria)'). Severity 'dependent' fits lifetime DSM-IV dependence. No other drug is named.

Note, no change: the second quote is the race-split sentence. The overall 6-year figure appears only in the sentence that lists the other drugs (number 2 quotes it with ellipses). Reading N=344 as 'already free' is still an inference from a table header, as the first reviewer said.

checked.label: hard: I can't handle quitting.
problems: All three quotes are word for word. Bonnet 2017 Figure 1 legend: 'The CWS usually lasts up to 3 weeks'. Connor 2022: 'Sleep disturbances may continue for several weeks or longer.' Allsop 2012 discussion: 'It is of note that the average level of functional impairment caused by cannabis withdrawal symptoms was relatively mild'. The fixed refs.2.cite holds: 49 non-treatment-seeking users who met DSM-IV dependence criteria, recruited in Sydney, with 'a one-hour psychological intervention and contingency management payments totalling AU$450'.

The proof gives only the average and is more hopeful than the source. The sentence right after the quote says 'the focus on average values ... masks the variation ... some study participants reported that cannabis withdrawal symptoms caused very high levels of functional impairment'. The authors expect treatment seekers to report more, and those more dependent reported more (p = 0.03). The reader who 'barely lasted three days' is the likely high-impairment case. The fix adds the spread within the 40-word limit (40 words).

fix.proof: Weed withdrawal usually lasts up to 3 weeks; poor sleep can last longer. In 49 people hooked on weed and paid to stay off for two weeks, harm to daily life was fairly mild on average, very high for some.

checked.label: need: Weed is the only thing that gets me to sleep.
problems: Holds. 'A high percentage (68.9%) of the study sample reported poor sleep quality' (PSQI > 5). The proof now states the comparison of change: 'compared to those without reductions in cannabis use, individuals who reduced use of cannabis over the trial demonstrated significantly greater reduction of anxiety, depression, and improvements of sleep quality over time'. The sleep slope is β = −0.07 (0.03)* in Model II, Table 3.
302 adults with DSM-IV cannabis dependence, 12 weeks. Severity 'dependent' fits. Proof: 33 words. Both quotes are word for word (13 and 22 words).

checked.label: plan step 3 proof: withdrawal time course (Budney 2003)
problems: Holds. The abstract: 18 marijuana users, 'a 5-day smoking-as-usual phase followed by a 45-day abstinence phase', after 'cessation of heavy cannabis (marijuana) use'. 'Onset typically occurred between Days 1-3, peak effects between Days 2-6, and most effects lasted 4-14 days.' The fixed text now says 'most lasted 4–14 days', which matches. 21 words. The quote is word for word (17 words). Only the abstract is open.

checked.label: plan step 4 proof: craving classes (Alias-Ferri 2026)
problems: Holds. In the full text the low class (n = 123, 41%) 'had the lowest mean baseline craving (M = 38.6). Craving then declined through three weeks after randomization before leveling off at week 4'. The moderate and decreasing class (38%) started at 'moderate (M = 55.2)' and 'saw large declines in the first four weeks'. Participants 'met ... DSM-IV ... criteria for cannabis dependence', N = 302, 12 weeks. 'All participants received contingency management (CM) ... CM reinforced both cannabis abstinence, confirmed by negative urine cannabinoid tests, and attendance'. 36 words. The quote is word for word (20 words).
Note, no change: the proof leaves out the other 21%, whose craving stayed moderate (11%) or high (10%). Those people had the worst outcomes. The proof is still not false; a reader can infer the rest.
